@@31468194 <p> How much does bovine eruction hurt the economy ? That is the key question that Minnesota Pollution Control Agency must answer after our state 's Court of Appeals ruled that by ignoring the effects of dairy cow eruction , flatulence and defecation on greenhouse gas emissions , the agency had erred in granting a permit . <p> Edward Lotterman <p> Eruction is the scientific term for belching . This is all about expansion of an already large family dairy farm near Lewiston in Winona County . <p> And there are very interesting economics in this issue . <p> Start with the gassy cows . All animals defecate and urinate . Ruminants , which include cattle , sheep , goats , deer , elk , giraffes , yaks , antelope , bison and camels , have a separate large stomach compartment , the rumen . It is a marvelous fermentation vat that can break down cellulose and extract nutrients that other vertebrates , including hogs and humans , can not . By turning otherwise indigestible plant materials into meat , milk , wool and leather , ruminants are of vital important to human life and benefit overall ecosystems in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a minor extent sheep , have played a key role in Minnesota agriculture since first European occupation of the land . The family dairy farm is the quintessential symbol of Minnesota agriculture and part of the heritage of millions in our state . But numbers of these traditional farms are shrinking fast . <p> The pollution problem is that fermentation of cellulose in rumens emits prodigious quantities of methane gas . Methane , also the principal component of natural gas , contains carbon and hence contributes to climate change . Cows belch enormous quantities of gas as they ruminate , while large quantities of flatulence come out the other end . <p> Excrement of all animals also produce much methane as it decomposes . Urine of all animals contains nitrogen , but that problem is a separate water pollution issue . <p> Domesticated ruminant methane emission is a big issue in the science of climate change and looms large in the cultural wars around this issue . " Get rid of all cows , become a vegan and drink soy or almond milk say , " an increasing number of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : " Whoa , Bossie ! " <p> Consideration of these emissions crosses a line in regulation of agricultural pollution . <p> A nauseously reeking hog facility may affect neighbors for a mile or two around . Livestock pollutants percolating into an aquifer may contaminate a large or small radius , depending on the quantity of pollutant and the size and geologic characteristics of the aquifer , but often are localized . Ditto for spills of liquid manure into lakes or streams . Large spills will have greater effects than small . The size and characteristics of the stream also are a factor . <p> So most of the external costs of livestock waste pollution are local or perhaps regional over several counties . To the extent that they affect large streams like the Minnesota River , they affect the whole state and eventually contribute to the dead zone in the Gulf of Mexico . <p> Regulation of greenhouse gas emissions is vastly different in that these affect the whole globe . It is a situation in which imposing costs from tighter regulation are very local , but the benefits @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the MPCA must now consider the effect of a 3,000-cow dairy on emissions of greenhouse gases in a unnecessary . It may still grant permission to go ahead for the expansion after doing this review , although the owners are also in a fight with their county authorities . <p> One must know that not all dairies are so regulated . All are part of a general category of " feedlots " that includes all livestock facilities for turkeys , hogs , beef feeding and anything else . Size is denominated in " animal units , " or AUs , so even llama or rabbit operations could be considered . <p> All facilities with over 50 AUs must be registered . A dairy cow is 1.4 AUs , but dairies also have calves and replacement heifers so two AUs per cow actually in the milking herd is a good rule of thumb . One beef cow or horse , three hogs , 10 sheep or 200 broilers also equal one AU . There are 24,000 such feedlots in the state @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sense across the political spectrum and keen political sensitivity to the rural vote combine to exempt most such farm facilities from regulation . Only some 1,300 are subject to state and/or federal supervision . The MCPA conducts about 2,000 inspections a year . Many are multiple inspections of a contentious or problem facility within one year . <p> The long-standing economic issue in all this is that of external costs . Raising livestock at any scale creates some level of pollution that affects others adversely . As a farm child in the 1950s and 1960s , I remember our creek ran brown in the spring ; farms were small and there were no regulations on runoff from manure piles or spreading manure on frozen sloping fields that would eventually thaw . <p> In the days when pollution control meant building higher smokestacks and engineers said " the solution to pollution is dilution , " farm animal runoff was diffused . Hog houses for 15 sows stank as did a pile of cow manure accumulated over a winter , at least once disturbed . But the radius was limited and there @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ mile . Town people lived in town and farmers lived on farms . <p> There were pollutants , but these were spread over a large area to absorb them . Our creek ran clear enough to see " clam " shells on the sandy bottom and " minnows " everywhere through all summer months . These were actually mussels and the now-endangered crystal darter . There were beavers , muskrats , mink and Great Blue herons . People with naturally high-nitrate wells and infants came to get water from our field drainage tile line . Some of these remain , but the stream is far more polluted than 50 years ago . <p> The MCPA must now consider if there are " diseconomies of scale . " Is more methane emitted from 3,000 cows in one facility than 150 cows on 25 or 30 farms ? The answer is no . Thus , as the structure of dairy farming consolidates , more cows will be regulated because ever-bigger operations will contain a growing percentage of all cows in the state . But methane directly emitted from cows wo n't . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . As one concentrates manure into enormous tanks , water pollution potential rises greatly . There are diseconomies of scale . But larger facilities also have the possibility of reducing methane emissions . <p> Biogas digesters that turn gases from decomposition of excrement into fuel gas have been around for decades on a small scale . For 10 cows or 50 , the cost of such equipment is high relative to value of fuel produced . But when you get to 1,500 or 3,000 cows , the per-cow cost shrinks and it becomes economical for farmers to install generator sets to produce electricity directly for the dairy operation or to feed back into the grid . There are economies of scale . But these installations are still rare . They do n't pencil out financially . <p> However , such calculations do not include the harm to the environment of simply venting off gases from manure pits . Put those into the equation and the bottom line changes . This would be an example of making the polluter face the total social cost of their facility and not just the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ forcing large livestock facilities to install such digesters and gensets . That is the " stick " approach and would generate intense opposition . <p> One could , however , use a " carrot . " Minnesota has had large subsidies to wind and solar power . It could subsidize methane digestion into fuel . Society would pay via taxes rather than through suffering the damages from pollution . It would shift the cost of methane emissions from decomposing manure from the world as a whole to the population of our state . This option needs more attention . <p> There also is the question of whether tighter regulations here will simply push dairying into less-regulated states with no reduction in overall methane emission from the dairy sector . Milk production and processing are rising rapidly in South Dakota , while dairying is shrinking here . @@31468497 <p> An international team of researchers has built a model that shows the possible simultaneous impact of global warming on agriculture and marine fisheries . In their paper published in the journal Science Advances , the group describes what their model showed developing over the rest of this century . <p> As global temperatures continue to rise ( just last week the World Meteorological Organization reported that greenhouse gas emission hit an all-time high last year ) as we humans fail to reduce the emission of greenhouse gases , scientists continue to carry out studies designed to help us better understand what will happen if we do not change our ways . In this new effort , the researchers have sought to demonstrate what will happen to our two main sources of food -- agriculture and fisheries -- when looked at simultaneously . They note that other studies have looked at the impact of climate change on both sources , but until now , none of them have looked at what will happen to food availability when both are impacted at the same time . <p> To gain a better perspective on what the future of agriculture and marine @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ century -- if greenhouse gas emissions remain unchanged -- the researchers built a model that took into account where food is grown or caught and likely impacts on production due to a changing climate . They also added in information that described the sensitivity of different areas to climate change -- areas in the tropics , for example , may not be able to adapt to warmer temperatures , while places like Canada and Russia might actually see increased food production . <p> The researchers report that the model showed that the worst-case scenario was rather dire -- 90 percent of the global population will be living in an area where production from agriculture and fisheries is falling by the end of this century . More specifically , the model showed a 25 percent reduction in average global productivity in the agriculture sector . For fisheries , the model showed declines of up to 60 percent . The researchers note that the model also showed different outcomes based on possible global warming mitigation efforts . They also noted that poorer countries will on average be more strongly impacted than richer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to copyright . The aim was to provide firewood , charcoal , fodder and timber to stabilize soil in degraded ecosystems and prevent desertification . <p> While the first introductions in Ethiopia were made during the 1970s and 1980s , problems soon arose in the early 1990s when the tree started invading croplands , grasslands , riverbanks and roadsides - causing significant environmental impacts and a source of conflict among pastoralist groups due to the effect on dwindling grazing land . <p> Mr Shiferaw said , " Our study provides evidence that land use and land cover changes in the Afar Region have led to a significant loss in ecosystem service values , with serious consequences for the livelihoods of the rural people . <p> " Negative net changes were found @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as a result of the Prosopis spreading so rapidly . @@31469994 <h> Sounds of the past give new hope for coral reef restoration <p> Young fish can be drawn to degraded coral reefs by loudspeakers playing the sounds of healthy reefs , according to new research published today in Nature Communications . <p> An international team of scientists from the UK 's University of Exeter and University of Bristol , and Australia 's James Cook University and Australian Institute of Marine Science , say this " acoustic enrichment " could be a valuable tool in helping to restore damaged coral reefs . <p> Working on Australia 's recently devastated Great Barrier Reef , the scientists placed underwater loudspeakers playing healthy reef recordings in patches of dead coral and found twice as many fish arrived - and stayed - compared to equivalent patches where no sound was played . <p> " Fish are crucial for coral reefs to function as healthy ecosystems , " said lead author Tim Gordon , of the University of Exeter . <p> " Boosting fish populations in this way could help to kick-start natural recovery processes , counteracting the damage we 're seeing on many coral reefs around the world . " <p> This new technique @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are quietened by degradation . <p> " Healthy coral reefs are remarkably noisy places - the crackle of snapping shrimp and the whoops and grunts of fish combine to form a dazzling biological soundscape . Juvenile fish home in on these sounds when they 're looking for a place to settle , " said senior author Professor Steve Simpson , also of the University of Exeter . <p> " Reefs become ghostly quiet when they are degraded , as the shrimps and fish disappear , but by using loudspeakers to restore this lost soundscape , we can attract young fish back again . <p> Australian Institute of Marine Science fish biologist Dr Mark Meekan added : " Of course , attracting fish to a dead reef wo n't bring it back to life automatically , but recovery is underpinned by fish that clean the reef and create space for corals to regrow . " <p> The study found that broadcasting healthy reef sound doubled the total number of fish arriving onto experimental patches of reef habitat , as well as increasing the number of species present by 50% . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ web - herbivores , detritivores , planktivores and predatory piscivores . <p> Different groups of fish provide different functions on coral reefs , meaning an abundant and diverse fish population is an important factor in maintaining a healthy ecosystem . <p> Professor Andy Radford , a co-author from the University of Bristol , said : " Acoustic enrichment is a promising technique for management on a local basis . <p> " However , we still need to tackle a host of other threats including climate change , overfishing and water pollution in order to protect these fragile ecosystems . " <p> Gordon added : " Whilst attracting more fish wo n't save coral reefs on its own , new techniques like this give us more tools in the fight to save these precious and vulnerable ecosystems . <p> " From local management innovations to international political action , we need meaningful progress at all levels to paint a better future for reefs worldwide . " <p> ### <p> The paper is entitled : " Acoustic enrichment can enhance fish community development on degraded coral reef habitat . @@82009294 <h> Wild animals evolving to give birth earlier in warming climate <p> Red deer on a Scottish island are providing scientists with some of the first evidence that wild animals are evolving to give birth earlier in the year as the climate warms . <p> Genetic changes to red deer on the Isle of Rum -- located off the west coast of Scotland -- have played a key role in a rapid shift in birth dates in recent years , new research shows . <p> Previous studies have shown that the deer have been giving birth earlier since the 1980s , at a rate of about three days per decade , partly due to the effects of warmer temperatures on the deer 's behaviour and physiology . <p> The study provides a rare example of evolution happening quickly enough to be detected over only a few decades . <p> A team including scientists from the University of Edinburgh made the discovery using field records and genetic data collected on Rum over a 45-year period since 1972 . <p> Female red deer -- called hinds -- give birth to a single calf each year , and those that reproduce earlier @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ researchers say . <p> Their findings show that this is partly because of an association between the genes that make hinds give birth earlier and higher overall reproductive success . As a result , genes for breeding earlier have become more common in the Rum deer population over time . <p> Red deer stag on the Isle of Rum , Scotland . Credit : Martyn Baker <p> The research , published in the journal PLOS Biology , involved scientists from the Australian National University and the universities of St Andrews and Cambridge . It was funded by the Natural Environment Research Council . The Isle of Rum National Nature Reserve is managed by Scottish Natural Heritage . <p> Dr. Timoth ? e Bonnet , of the Australian National University , who led the study , said : " This is one of the few cases where we have documented evolution in action , showing that it may help populations adapt to climate warming . " <p> Professor Josephine Pemberton , of the University of Edinburgh 's School of Biological Sciences , who was also involved in the study , said @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the few ways to understand how populations respond to environmental change and how to manage its effects . " <p> Sally Thomas , Scottish Natural Heritage 's Director of People and Nature , said : " These findings are a fascinating example of the impact climate change may be having on wildlife . More and more research is demonstrating climate change is influencing species across the UK and the world . " <p> This document is subject to copyright . In the meantime , to ensure continued support , we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript . <h> Subjects <h> Abstract <p> The international community has treated climate change as an emissions reduction challenge , drawing on the analytical metaphor of the global commons , and thus the politics of collective action and international cooperation . So far , these strategies have failed to produce an effective global response . We propose decarbonization as the defining challenge and a new guiding metaphor for the problem structure : the global fractal . This metaphor aptly describes the decarbonization challenge , capturing the multilevel and interdependent nature of carbon lock-in and the fractal carbon trap facing decarbonization efforts . It also provides a means to explore the range of diverse policies and practices that can potentially escape the fractal carbon trap and catalyse deep decarbonization . <h> Acknowledgements <p> The authors were supported @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Council of Canada . @@82183298 <h> Experts question study claiming to pinpoint birthplace of all humans <p> A new genetic study suggests all modern humans trace our ancestry to a single spot in southern Africa 200,000 years ago . But experts say the study , which analyzes the DNA of living people , is not nearly comprehensive enough to pinpoint where our species arose . <p> " I 'm persuaded that southern Africa was an important area for human evolution , " says population geneticist Aylwyn Scally of the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom who was not involved with the work . But , he says , studies of living people 's DNA ca n't reveal the precise location of our ancestors . " It would be astonishing if all our genetic ancestry at this time arose in one small homeland . " <p> Modern humans arose in Africa at least 250,000 to 300,000 years ago , fossils and DNA reveal . But scientists have been unable to pinpoint a more specific homeland because the earliest Homo sapiens fossils are found across Africa , and ancient DNA from African fossils is scarce and not old enough . <p> In the new study @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ groups whose DNA is poorly known , including foragers and hunter-gatherers in Namibia and South Africa who speak Khoisan languages with click consonants . The authors analyzed the mitochondrial DNA ( mtDNA ) , a type of DNA inherited only from mothers , and compared it to mtDNA in databases from more than 1000 other Africans , mostly from southern Africa . Then the researchers sorted how all the samples were related to each other on a family tree . <p> Confirming earlier studies , the data reveal that one mtDNA lineage in the Khoisan speakers -- L0 -- is the oldest known mtDNA lineage in living people . The work also tightens the date of origin of L0 to about 200,000 years ago ( with a range of error of 165,000 to 240,000 ; previous studies had a range of error from 150,000 to 250,000 ) , the team reports today in Nature . Because today this lineage is found only in people in southern Africa , people carrying the L0 lineage lived in southern Africa and formed the ancestral population for all living humans , says lead author @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Medical Research and the University of Sydney in Australia . <p> Vanessa Hayes has long studied the Ju'hoansi of the Kalahari Desert of Namibia who speak a Khoisan click language . <p> Specifically , Hayes and her colleagues argue that the homeland was in what is now the Kalahari region of northern Botswana . Although the Kalahari is mostly desert and salt flats today , it was a lush wetland from 200,000 to 130,000 years ago near what would have been the largest lake in Africa , according to climate data and simulations in the study . <p> The team proposes that people with the L0 mtDNA thrived in their Kalahari homeland until about 130,000 to 110,000 years ago , when climate change opened green corridors to the northeast and southwest . Some individuals left their homeland and evolved new mtDNA lineages that the team identifies . <p> But mtDNA alone in living people is a poor tool for tracking ancient population history in Africa , says evolutionary geneticist Sarah Tishkoff of the University of Pennsylvania . MtDNA traces only one genetic lineage passed from mothers to their children over @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Y chromosomes inherited from fathers or of any nuclear genes inherited from both parents , they might have gotten many different answers , Scally adds . <p> Hayes responds that the team chose mtDNA because it does n't get shuffled in early fetal development like other types of DNA do . As a result , it can be used to trace living people 's evolution in a direct line to a small number of female ancestors who only lived in southern Africa , she says . " It acts like a time capsule for our ancestral mothers . " Most of the data on Khoisan speakers ' Y chromosomes has disappeared as men mixed with other groups , she says . <p> Critics also warn that the female ancestors of the Khoisan speakers may not have lived in the same place 200,000 years ago . The ancestral women with the L0 lineage could have migrated to southern Africa from elsewhere or been part of a larger population whose descendants outside of southern Africa went extinct , Tishkoff says . <p> The bottom line , says population geneticist Pontus Skoglund of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ move and mix so much over the millennia that studying DNA from living humans is " very limited when it comes to reconstructing what happened to populations 70,000 to 200,000 years ago . " For that , he says , you need ancient DNA . Or well-dated fossils .

@@82245798 <h> I 'd be skeptical if I were you <p> George Will , veteran journalist and social analyst , intoned in his avuncular way , " The strongest continuous thread in America 's political tradition is skepticism . " While looking for virtues suitable to a country in political and social disarray , I could n't help but be particularly happy at the thought of nominating skepticism as the electoral foundation of the future . <p> It seems to me that , instead of scrutinizing the promises that come from politicians in an election year , we simply take for granted that what they say is true , that what they promise is doable . So , we vote with certainty without examining what could certainly happen if we got what we say we want . <p> And when we do n't get what we were told we 'd get , we blame everybody but our most gullible selves for the perverse situations political hyperbole spawns . We buy into fantasy and blame it on everybody but ourselves and our greed , ourselves and our misogyny , ourselves and our disinterest in the needs of the rest of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ spread by elections . Few voters make the effort to compare one political promise with another , let alone assess the probable effects of them on other important programs . At the last election , for instance , we voted to bring American industries back to America . An iota of awareness could have alerted us to the fact that just about nothing is made exclusively -- let alone totally -- anywhere in this interlocking global world . We all make parts for things everybody else makes and then we all sell them to one another . Which is what keeps creativity alive , money moving and the economy growing , but it does not re-create a world long gone . <p> Truly , no one is an island anymore . Commerce is the peace plan of a global age . It is the only spiritual proof a secular world has that we really do need one another . <p> And yet , that kind of narrow-minded political dogmatism becomes the overriding electoral political value -- not our needs , not our budget . Instead , we spread out our @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the certainty that they are about to pull our White Rabbit out of the voting machine . With no data whatsoever to support a candidate 's claims , the various political parties woo us to vote for this year 's " America 's Got Talent " nominees with all the glitz and glamour -- and eventual disappearing act -- that implies . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> As a result , the ability to be certain about an aspirant 's commitment to the issues of the age , as well as the quality of their characters or the effectiveness of their proposals , go too often unexamined . And with it , the likelihood that what candidates guarantee is really possible becomes at least slim , if not totally speculative . <p> All they need to do , it seems , is to feed our wildest dreams . <p> For instance : <p> Fossil fuels , we 're asked to believe , are coming back as the savior of the country 's economic backbone simply because a candidate says , like God the Creator , " Let there be light @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ But what about the collision course between fossil fuels and climate change , global warming , desertification , flooding and the massive immigration that occurs when people live near flood-prone rivers or coastlines , or on dry and sterile and fruitless land ? What makes us think that industries given over to robots and pollution and computerization will ever bring back the corporations of the past as they once were ? Like buggy whips , for instance . Or dry wells . Or the fossil fuels of one industrial era to power -- and threaten -- a newer one ? <p> I 'd be skeptical if I were you . <p> Or what about the warning that the country is being overrun by foreign robbers or rapists , muggers and murderers from which only a countrywide wall can save us . <p> Question : How many people -- what percentage -- of foreigners who have walked into the country across the river from us have really committed crimes here other than speeding tickets , perhaps ? <p> In fact , Jennifer Doleac in " Are Immigrants More Likely to Commit @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and approaches have also concluded that immigrants are generally less likely to commit crimes . Citing data from a recent study that looks specifically at flows of immigrants from Mexico , she points out that Mexican immigration has no effect on violent or property crime in the United States . In fact , most undocumented aliens , various Homeland Security reports attest , have been in jail for foreign reasons : meaning they 've been put in jail because they 're here without documentation . And so the merry-go-round of political racism goes on . <p> We did that once with the Indians , the African Americans , the Irish and the Eastern Europeans . You can see how that worked out . <p> But we go on our certain ways , selecting candidates by party affiliation and personal promises rather than on the basis of the effect of their values , beliefs and judgments on the Constitution . As in , money allocated by Congress for the upgrading of the U.S. military has been moved without congressional approval to build a wall most of the country does not want @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tampering with the laws and values of the nation , what else will they do to distort the other democratic values our Founders left us ? <p> I 'd be skeptical if I were you . <p> Once a Constitution can be ignored so blithely , nothing else is safe . <p> Unfortunately , that 's not the only problem that comes with political fantasies or political lies . <p> It is one thing to get the political version of snake oil by failing to exercise the skepticism necessary to save ourselves from buyer 's remorse after an election . But quite another serious concern is the emerging data on the effect of the deliberate implantation of false information . <p> Elizabeth Loftus , one of the country 's ranking psychological researchers in memory development for more than 25 years and holder of the Western Psychological Association 's " Lifetime Achievement Award , " warns us that the deliberate implantation of false memories -- lies -- can affect a person 's behavior in the future . <p> The attitudes created , for instance , in American children from the negative @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ during the Cold War has left U.S.-Russian relationships at a disadvantage to this day . <p> Hardly a grade school child of the ' 50s has forgotten being ordered to crawl under a desk during " air raid drills " designed to save them from atomic bombs . Those bombs , we were told , with one enemy only recently vanquished , could well be dropped on us , this time by Russia . <p> A little more skepticism , perhaps , could have saved us from decades of nuclear hysteria . A little less labeling might have left us with a little less East-West tension . A little less enmity , a little more peace and prosperity . <p> From where I stand , in fact , it is groundless , false enmity that we are suffering from right now . And it is being stoked by actors most advantaged by a country in fear of the unknown . <p> Skepticism , a healthy dose of scrutiny and uncertainty , may well save the world from more political charlatans than the world ever dreamed . Then , perhaps , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , more in tune with the kind of political status that is gained by being publicly moral , publicly nonpartisan and publicly committed to the needs of the entire nation rather than simply half of it . <p> The question , of course , is whether we ourselves are wary enough to distinguish universal good from just one more set of frangible fantasies when we see them . <p> Judging from recent history , I 'd be a bit skeptical about that , if I were you . <p> Joan Chittister is a Benedictine sister of Erie , Pennsylvania . <p> Editor 's note : We can send you an email alert every time Joan Chittister 's column , From Where I Stand , is posted to NCRonline.org . @@82259495 <h> Farmers can play a role in reducing atmospheric carbon Letter <p> I am increasingly impressed by the potential of land-based methods of carbon drawdown to mitigate climate change . Many of these practices could be applied on farms large or small , conventional or organic . <p> Interspersing trees with food crops or livestock animals adds diversity of nutrients to the soil . Planting cover crops such as clover , hairy vetch and rye carry nitrogen from the atmosphere into the soil . Rotational grazing ( allowing cows or other ruminant animals to intensively graze a pasture , then moving them to adjacent fresh pasture to allow the first one to regrow ) adds significant fertility to soil . Planting trees in the pasture increases soil carbon even more . <p> No-till farming and permaculture ( working with nature 's systems to create multi-layered , compact food gardens with minimal machinery or other disturbance ) are among many ecological agriculture practices that partner with Earth and soak up atmospheric carbon . <p> Plants are carbon storehouses . While living , they turn carbon dioxide into sugar and energy ; when they die , their decomposed bodies permanently store @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ occurs ) .

@@82291295 <h> Two new analyses : significant benefits for Pennsylvania from historic move to limit carbon pollution <p> Two new analyses show significant opportunities for Pennsylvania under environmental protections that are compatible with the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative -- commonly known as RGGI . <p> RGGI is a collaboration of nine northeast states that is designed to lower carbon pollution from the power sector . That order followed Wolf 's commitment to reducing Pennsylvania 's climate pollution by 26 percent by 2025 and 80 percent by mid-century , compared to 2005 levels . <p> Pennsylvania has the fifth dirtiest power sector in the nation , and the power plants operating in Pennsylvania emit more carbon pollution than all the other power plants in the nine northeastern states in RGGI combined . @@82392093 <p> The recent special issue on Mountain Life ( 13 September , p. 1092 ) and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate ( 1 ) have highlighted the extent of climate change impacts in mountain environments . Globally , there is also increasing evidence for elevation-dependent warming ( EDW ) , the amplification of warming at higher elevations compared with surrounding lowlands resulting from both local feedback processes and altered patterns of meridional heat transport ( 2 -- 4 ) . However , our ability to detect EDW remains limited because there are sparse meteorological records from higher elevations in most parts of the world . <p> The Global Historical Climatology Network Monthly -- Version 3 lists only 84 weather stations above 2000 m . They are spread across 20 countries , but 68% of them are located in either the southern Rocky Mountains or greater Tibetan Plateau ( 5 ) . There are many geographical gaps . For example , the vast mountainous regions of western Canada have few weather stations above the median elevation of glaciers ( about 2190 m in southern British Columbia and Alberta @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ current station in Canada above 1300 m ( Banff ) ( 5 ) . <p> Ground observations are essential for understanding changes occurring at higher elevation . They can not be replaced entirely by either remote sensing or climate reanalysis data because proxy observations are biased depending on external factors such as the extent of snow cover ( 7 , 8 ) . Informal meteorological stations have been established for a variety of research and avalanche forecasting purposes , but these are insufficient to address the EDW data gap . The World Meteorological Organization Global Cryosphere Watch program ( 9 ) has developed standards that should be adopted internationally , and we strongly encourage the establishment of comprehensive and sustained high-elevation meteorological monitoring networks in order to properly study the influences of climate change on mountain environments .

@@82394098 <h> Shell is test-driving a number of eco-friendly business models before deciding which one to buy into <p> Royal Dutch Shell RDS.B 0.33% knows that climate change means business change , but is n't sure how . Like a savvy car buyer , it is testing out a few eco-friendly models before it chooses one . <p> The approach is sensible for Europe 's most valuable oil and gas producer , given that we do n't know what a lower-carbon future really looks like . At some point , though , investors need to brace for a big decision . <p> All countries except the U.S. have promised to cut their carbon emissions to comply with the 2015 Paris climate accord . Extreme weather events , ongoing climate protests and shifting public opinion are now pushing governments to deliver . The oil and gas business is on the front line of the drastic economic changes required . <p> Equally , though , there is great uncertainty about the pace of the transition and how lower-carbon economies will eventually be structured to produce and sell power , food and transportation . <p> Faced with this conundrum , Shell has promised @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2016 level . It has gradually moved away from oil toward lower-carbon gas and has been adding electricity to its product mix . It is also applying its trading and retailing expertise to products other than oil and gas . With 45,000 stores -- more than Starbucks or McDonalds -- Shell serves 30 million customers daily . <p> In recent years , the company also has invested an average of between $1 billion and $2 billion annually on small-scale experiments in new energy sources including power , biofuels , solar , wind , batteries and hydrogen . Most do n't make a profit , but do n't cost too much relative to the more than $20 billion a year that Shell generates in free cash flow . <p> The experiments give the company information about new markets and the opportunity to shape customer expectations and regulations as they develop . More speculatively , they could also provide a first mover advantage in lower-carbon businesses that might eventually deliver the big profits oil and gas investors expect . <p> Some see the low-carbon projects as " greenwashing " Shell 's fossil @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ its capital spending . But that is to underestimate the massive investment required for one of the world 's top oil producers to halve its carbon emissions . <p> Flags and graffiti cover the entrance to the headquarters of Royal Dutch Shell in London during an Extinction Rebellion protest in April . @@82397690 <h> Summary <p> Holding a major international summit on climate change against a backdrop of civil discontent like the kind that has rocked Chile might have given the world the impression that issues like clean energy can be addressed without also confronting problems of social justice . So last month , in the midst of massive protests on cost-of-living burdens and other inequalities , Chile withdrew as the host nation of the United Nations Climate Change Conference ( COP25 ) . Instead , COP25 will convene next week in Madrid , Spain . Despite this decision , Chile 's commitment to maintain its presidency of COP25 through next year hopefully signals a turning point in climate action -- one that further steers Chile and the rest of the global community to recognize connections between social and climate crises , and to support climate policies that do not leave anyone behind .
